tells: The point-cloud and photogrammetry street scenes are deliberately broken: kaleidoscopic building rings and melting terrain. This is an authored aesthetic, not a default effect.
A specific idea links the frames: one captured place is rebuilt, inverted and turned into code or text. The lettered point-cloud frame ties the type to the space.
There is a lot of variety: tunnel view, sky view looking up, a mangled landscape, a monochrome text field. The camera behaviour implies real choreography.
The finish is rough and the palette is noisy (hot red and yellow against grey and blue). It reads as experimental music-video or art work rather than polished studio work.
gaps: The colour has no discipline. The saturated red/yellow grading fights the image, while D holds one controlled warm palette throughout.
The text frame is monospace scattered over the geometry with no hierarchy or legibility. The type needs a deliberate point of view.
The finish is uneven: smeared meshes and blown highlights look accidental rather than designed. Glitch frames need the same compositional control as D's strongest frames.

tells: A distinctive idea that belongs to this piece alone: a clockwork map of the world that builds itself, telling the geography and politics of the series with tactile miniatures.
Every frame is a poster. The engraved astrolabe band, the cities rising out of gears, and the parchment map with an inked river all have dense, layered detail and shallow depth of field.
Real light and material: a warm sun-flare core, aged metal, wood and parchment, and a consistent amber-and-umber palette.
The typography fits the world: a classical serif with small caps, credits tucked into the scene next to heraldic sigils, and a dragon-flanked title lockup.
The movement is choreographed: a crane over the map, mechanisms unfolding, and the title resolving in the central sun. The variety of shots is held together by one system.
gaps: The credit type is very small and sometimes gets lost in busy, detailed backgrounds. It could hold more contrast against them.
The end-title lockup is centred and symmetrical, more conventional than the inventive map sequences before it.
The heavy warm grade and blooming flare flatten some midtones. A slightly wider tonal range would bring out more of the material detail.

tells: The logo is a real object: the N's ribbon breaks into light strands, and frame 2 shows its stem already splitting into fibres before the dive

Choreography carries over between frames: a tight logo becomes a full-frame flight through vertical bands, which opens into a perspective tunnel of coloured light, which pulls back to the reformed N, so the shot loops back on itself
The palette is planned: the red-on-black brand colours open into a broad spectrum (magenta, cyan, violet, amber) only in the middle of the piece and then close back to red
The light strands have glow, depth fog and a faint star field behind them, so there is real light and depth here, not flat gradient bars
There is no headline type, because the mark itself does the typographic work, and the custom N carries the whole piece
gaps: The opening and closing frames sit on plain black with a centred mark. That is correct for a logo ident, but it leaves no frame-level texture or setting at the bookends
As a brand sting it is built around a logo rather than a story, so it gives less to read than C's narrative world-building
The colour-spectrum tunnel is a familiar light-streak idea, and it is the execution rather than the concept that lifts it

tells: It works with photogrammetry and point-cloud data in a specific, deliberate way: scanned brick streets are turned inside out, folded into an Inception-style ring of houses around a radial blade structure, and pushed into a spiky displaced terrain
Frame 4 builds monospace text into the point-cloud architecture. It reads as a fragment of a monologue about point clouds and simulation, so the type is part of the concept and is not a caption

The frames vary a great deal: a red thermal-style alley, a crushed landscape under a sky, an upward fish-eye shot of a vortex against a fire-lit sky, a black void of text, then a return to the alley. That suggests a camera path through one connected scanned world
Experimental, art-video sensibility; nothing about it is template-like
gaps: Its finish is rough on purpose but uneven: the red alleys are muddy and lack hierarchy, while C makes every frame read as a poster
Colour feels like a by-product of the data rather than a designed palette (saturated red/yellow artifacts vs. a muted earthy world), so a controlled grade would unify it
The text treatment in frame 4 has a concept but no typographic finish (default-looking monospace, random scale), so it needs a considered face and a rhythm for the layout

tells: It has an idea only this piece could have: the show's geography is a clockwork map whose cities unfold mechanically, a world-model that also acts as an orrery
Its materials are tactile: engraved bronze, wood, bone-like spires, gears and parchment, all with real specular light, shallow depth of field and atmospheric haze
The astrolabe band in the first and last frames is lit by a blazing sun inside the sphere, and engraved reliefs on it tell the backstory, so the bookends rhyme
Credits are integrated into the world: small Trajan-like caps placed beside each sigil, scaled to sit in the set rather than over it
The title lockup is a custom, beautifully set cartouche in which the 'OF' is set small between the two words, with rich bevel and glow that suits the period
The palette is restrained (warm bronze, ivory, slate, parchment green), and the frames move from macro to aerial map to mechanism, which shows choreographed camera language
gaps: It is the benchmark entry here, so it has no major gaps
Credits are small and low-contrast against busy detail in places (frame 2), which costs some legibility
The final lockup is a little more conventional and glossy than the inventiveness of the mechanical sequences before it

defects: Effectively one 17.6s continuous procedural shot: the pace FAIL comes from a single simulation evolving, not from directed shots. The 0.17s median comes from flicker in the noise, not from cuts.
The opening noise field (frame 1) and the near-empty flat-line frame (frame 5) are visually dead: low information, and neither works as a held image.
The fine horizontal line raster sits close to pixel pitch, so moiré and shimmer are likely on downscale or compression; the pairs frames already show beating in the ring regions.
Red accent peaks are soft additive blobs pasted onto the lines rather than light the lines catch. Their placement looks random, not choreographed.
SIGNAL lockup: the slatted letterforms are a stock 'type through scanlines' treatment, and the grey ring ghost behind them reads muddy and low-contrast.

Audio: the first ~6s is three near-identical filtered noise bursts separated by hard gaps, so it is static and repetitive. The riser is a plain exponential noise sweep, and the tail ticks decay mechanically.
gaps: Motion has no authored timing: the wave field morphs at a constant, sim-driven rate with no anticipation, holds or accents. Top work would choreograph the noise→interference→order transition in beats, with distinct shots, camera or scale changes, and a hard, designed handoff from the waveform to the wordmark.

Sound is thin generated design: white-noise bursts, a textbook riser and one broadband hit, with almost no tonal or harmonic content and no layered foley for the line material. A top studio would build a produced score whose partials resolve from noise to pitch alongside the picture.

Finish and image-making: the moiré-prone raster, flat black field without lighting, glow-blob accents and a generic slatted end title fall short of poster-grade frames. It needs real light falloff on the lines, controlled line density versus resolution, and a final lockup that grows from the system instead of being stamped over it.
